title: How to Photograph Beer for Instagram | Craft Beer School
desc: Light, glass, foam, condensation and phone settings for beer photos that look like the real pour, plus what India's ad rules mean for your feed.
teaser: A flat brown pint on a dark table sells nothing. Five minutes of light and timing fixes most of it.
standfirst: Good beer photos are mostly about light and timing, not cameras. Here is how we shoot a pour so it looks the way it tastes, using a phone and a window.
sections: Why most beer photos look flat

Beer is a liquid you see through. Shoot it the way you would shoot a plate of food, lit from the front. The light bounces off the glass and the beer turns into a dull brown block. The colour that makes a pale ale glow or a stout look like polished wood only appears when light passes through the liquid.

So the first rule is simple. Put the light behind or beside the glass, never behind the camera. A window works better than any lamp you own. On a bright day, sit the glass a metre from a north or east facing window, shoot across it at a slight angle and watch the beer change colour on your screen.
Glass, pour and the 30 second window

Use clean glassware that suits the style. A tulip for a hazy IPA, a tall weizen glass for a wheat beer, a straight pint or a stange for a lager. Wash it, rinse it with cold water and polish the outside with a lint free cloth. Fingerprints show up badly once light passes through the glass.

Pour for the camera, not for drinking. A firm pour into the centre of a tilted glass, straightened at the end, gives two to three fingers of head. That head starts collapsing almost at once, so have the shot framed before you pour. In practice you get about 30 seconds of good foam. Shoot a burst and pick the best frame afterwards.

If the beer will not hold a head at all, that is a brewing message, not a photography problem. Our guide to tasting beer covers what foam tells you.
Condensation and the Indian humidity trap

Condensation says cold and fresh. In most of India you get it for free: take a can from a cold room at 2 to 4 °C into a Mumbai or Chennai summer and it beads in seconds. The trouble is that it then runs into streaks and puddles on the table within a minute or two.

Wipe the can, let it bead again and shoot in the first minute. For a product shot that needs to last, food stylists mist the surface with a mix of glycerine and water, which forms droplets that stay put. If you do this, use an empty can or a sealed one that nobody will drink from.

• Tap to focus on the beer, then pull exposure down. Phones expose for the bright window and blow out the highlights. Dropping exposure a stop keeps the colour rich.
  • Turn off the flash. It flattens the beer and puts a hot spot on the glass.
  • Use the 2x lens, not the wide lens. Wide lenses distort a glass and make it look like it is leaning away from you.
  • Shoot at eye level with the glass for pours and from above for flat lays with cans, labels and food.
  • Edit lightly. Warmth and contrast, nothing more. Over saturated amber looks fake. Anyone who drinks your beer will notice the difference in the glass.

A beer alone on a white table is a catalogue shot. Context gives it a story. Put it next to a plate of the food you serve it with in the taproom, a hand holding the glass, the brew kit blurred in the background or a bag of the malt that went into it. Keep the props few and honest. A pile of hops that never touched the recipe is the kind of detail a beer drinker spots.

Shoot people from behind or at an angle where faces do not matter, unless you have their permission. Never show anyone who could look under age. Never show drinking alongside driving, machinery or the pool.
What India's advertising rules mean for your feed

Direct advertising of alcohol is restricted in India. Platforms add their own rules for alcohol content on top. Breweries handle this in different ways: age gated accounts, posts about the taproom, food and events rather than offers on beer, with no discounts or price promotions in captions. Enforcement varies and the rules change, so read our guide to alcohol advertising rules in India and check with someone who knows the current position before you plan a paid campaign.

The photos still matter for all of this. A good picture of a pour on your own account is often what makes someone visit the taproom. What to post, how often and how to measure it is covered in social media marketing for breweries.
Build a small shot list and repeat it

Consistency beats talent here. Pick one window, one table surface and one time of day. Shoot every new release there. Your grid starts to look like a brand instead of a random album. A short list we use for any new beer:

  1. Hero pour, backlit, eye level.
  2. Can or bottle with condensation, label sharp.
  3. Flat lay with the food pairing.
  4. A hand holding the glass in the taproom.
  5. A detail shot of the foam or the colour against the light.

Five photos, twenty minutes and you have a week of posts. The harder question is what the label, the glass and the photo say together, which is where branding starts to matter more than technique.
faqs: Do I need a proper camera to photograph beer?
No. A recent phone, a window and a clean glass get you most of the way. Light and timing make far more difference than the camera.
Why does my beer look brown and dull in photos?
The light is probably coming from behind the camera. Move the light behind or beside the glass so it passes through the beer and the colour shows.
Can a brewery post beer photos on Instagram in India?

Many do, but direct alcohol advertising is restricted and platforms have their own alcohol policies. Rules vary and change, so check the current position before posting offers or running paid campaigns.
